posts.title: How Makerspaces Get Started
posts.description: (Disclaimer – all words are my own, I used my AI agent to suggest tweaks for readability & organization) The purpose of this article is to sort of tell the story of my experiences with public makerspaces, and offer some advice for the very first steps. It can be a long journey from idea to execution. But you can do it! Story First Before I start, I should disclaim that I likely am not an “expert” in starting makerspaces. But then again, there aren’t a lot of resources out there for starting makerspaces, and I think it’s still worth giving my perspective. In about 2017, I got some of the entrepreneurial spirit. I was in grad school, and I wanted to start a company that sold circuit mills. My idea linked back to this idea that 3D printing was so big because all you needed was a machine and filament, then you could download whatever model you wanted. posts.title: Running Makerspace Events
posts.description: (Disclaimer – all words are my own, I used my AI agent to suggest tweaks for readability & organization) Why Are Events Important for a Makerspace? Why are events important for a makerspace? Why am I starting off with that rather than safety, space organization, business strategy, etc.? Well, a makerspace is nothing without users, and users need a reason to come into the space. For something like the Alley Makerspace, some class work, like Engineering Fundamentals, pulls students in. Capstone / Enterprise is another component. But only a small fraction of students come into the space just because they have a project and they want to work on it. The job of a successful makerspace operator is to get people in the door, get them engaged, and then get them coming back. You can do that with two things: Really useful tools Events Events can be a lot cheaper. But events take work, and careful, careful consideration. posts.title: Why Blogging is Important
posts.description: Blogging is such a 2004 thing to do. Why do it? No one reads this crap anyway. I suppose that’s something I tell myself, however I find that genuine blogs can be a way out of the “enshitification” of the internet. It can be a way to share your body of ideas & work in one spot – to really put on display who you are. Usually I discover other peoples blogs through websites like Hackaday , and I love browsing through some of the zany projects and ideas people share in their own little corner of the internet. In contrast if I go on a website like Reddit, everything is all homogeneous, same format same style, same “Reddit-accepted voice”. In addition the internet is chalk full of AI. Half the time I’m scrutinizing if what I’m reading was made by a real person more than actually just enjoying seeing someone’s thoughts.
